summary.en: Generate distinct arrangements with swaps or a used array, and produce lexicographic output without duplicates.
summary.bn: swap বা used অ্যারে দিয়ে আলাদা সাজানো ক্রম বানাও, আর একই অক্ষরের জন্য বাড়তি উত্তর ছাপানো এড়াও।

notes: The demonstrated programs use C17; the lesson states their input and arithmetic bounds.

sections.title: Fix a prefix with a reversible swap
One letter, all equal, and no letters

examples.title: Generate distinct words by swapping
examples.explanationHtml: Input aba prints aba, aab and baa. This order follows the current suffix arrangement and is not lexicographic. Every child restores its swap so later candidates see the correct remaining word.

examples.title: Generate in lexicographic order
examples.explanationHtml: The sorted used-array method prints aab, aba and baa for the same input. Its insertion-sort preparation is deliberately small and explicit. The output buffer receives a terminator before each complete word is printed.

examples.title: Count arrangements of repeated letters
examples.explanationHtml: For aabb, the program divides 4! by 2! for the two a copies and 2! for the two b copies. It prints six. This fixed calculation illustrates the formula without attempting large factorial arithmetic.

practice.title: Trace swap-based generation for aba, keeping only distinct branches.
practice.statementHtml: Trace swap-based generation for aba, keeping only distinct branches.
hints: Begin with the state and the input conditions.
practice.answerHtml: At the root choose a from index zero: its suffix produces aba then aab. Next choose b: the remaining aa gives baa once. Skip the final root a because that value was already tried there. The result order is aba, aab, baa.

practice.title: Compute the number of distinct arrangements of aabb and explain the denominator.
practice.statementHtml: Compute the number of distinct arrangements of aabb and explain the denominator.
hints: Begin with the state and the input conditions.
practice.answerHtml: Four labelled positions give 4!=24 arrangements. Exchanging the two a copies changes no visible word, as does exchanging the two b copies. Divide by 2! times 2! to obtain 6 distinct words.

quiz.prompt: For distinct items, how many length-four permutations exist?
quiz.explanation: The choices decrease from four to three to two to one, giving 4 factorial.

quiz.prompt: What must happen after a swap-based recursive child returns?
quiz.explanation: Undo restores the suffix before trying another candidate at this position.

quiz.prompt: Why is seen reset for each recursive depth?
options: Equal values need only one choice per position
No repeated letter is ever legal
A global set sorts the word
quiz.explanation: A letter may reappear at later positions, but identical alternatives at one position duplicate branches.

quiz.prompt: Which preparation is needed by the lexicographic used-array method?
quiz.explanation: Trying sorted available letters at each level orders the complete words lexicographically.

quiz.prompt: For sorted aab, which equal-copy rule avoids duplicate branches?
options: Skip a only at the leaf
Skip a later equal copy when the previous copy is unused
Skip the previous copy when it is used
quiz.explanation: The earlier identical copy represents this choice first; after it is used, another copy may fill a later position.

quiz.prompt: How many distinct strings can aaa produce?
quiz.explanation: All six labelled reorderings spell the same visible string.

quiz.prompt: What dominates the cost of printing n! distinct permutations?
options: Writing n characters for each permutation
quiz.explanation: Even an efficient generator needs at least n times n! character writes.

quiz.prompt: What string remains after swapping positions zero and one twice?
quiz.explanation: The second swap reverses the first swap exactly.

quiz.prompt: How many root choices survive local duplicate filtering for aba?
quiz.explanation: Only the distinct root letters a and b create branches.

quiz.prompt: What distinct-permutation count does the aabb factorial quotient print?
quiz.explanation: Each pair of equal letters contributes a factorial-two divisor.

keyPoints.en: A permutation places every item in an ordered position.
keyPoints.bn: পারমুটেশনে প্রতিটি আইটেম একটা নির্দিষ্ট পজিশনে বসে।

keyPoints.en: Swap back after each recursive branch.
keyPoints.bn: প্রতিটি রিকার্সিভ পথ শেষে swap করে আগের অবস্থা ফেরাও।

keyPoints.en: A local seen set skips repeated choices at one depth.
keyPoints.bn: একই ধাপে seen সেট দিয়ে একই অক্ষর আবার নেওয়া এড়াও।

keyPoints.en: Sorted candidates with a used array give lexicographic order.
keyPoints.bn: সাজানো অক্ষর আর used অ্যারে দিয়ে lexicographic ক্রমে উত্তর পাও।

keyPoints.en: Duplicate values reduce the number of distinct arrangements.
keyPoints.bn: একই মান একাধিকবার থাকলে আলাদা সাজানো ক্রমের সংখ্যা কমে।

examQuestions.question: State the invariant and justify the time and space costs of Generating Permutations.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
For swapping, the invariant is that the prefix is fixed and the suffix contains exactly the remaining multiset of characters. Swapping one candidate into the next position preserves that multiset contract for the child. Swapping back restores it for the parent.

Equal characters chosen at the same position leave the same remaining multiset. Exploring one such choice therefore covers every distinct continuation that any equal copy could produce. A local seen set removes duplicates without removing distinct words.

For the used-array method, used[i] says whether candidate index i already occupies an earlier output position. The duplicate rule forces identical copies to be consumed in index order. Every distinct word has exactly one such canonical labelled construction. Trying candidate values in increasing order makes the first differing character determine output order.

With n distinct characters, printing n! words of length n requires at least Omega(n*n!) character writes. The search tree and its candidate loops fit O(n*n!) time for these straightforward generators. Initial O(n^2) insertion sorting is negligible compared with large factorial output.

The swap method uses O(n) stack depth. Its per-call seen table has constant size for this fixed alphabet, so total auxiliary space remains O(n). The used-array method has candidate, used and result arrays plus the same linear-depth stack.

With repeated multiplicities c1,c2,..., the number of distinct words is n! divided by the product of their factorials. The lower bound becomes n times that count for printing. Searching can still include rejected candidate checks; an output-count formula alone does not describe every operation.
